detail: supported
- Voxel data size: 15 bytes per voxel (3×4 bytes position + 3 bytes normal) [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the voxel data size is 15 bytes per voxel, consisting of 3x4 bytes for position and 3 bytes for normal. The evidence in Source [S1], specifically in section '3.3 Data Encoding', explicitly states: 'Assuming that we have three four-byte values for position and three bytes for normal-information, 15 bytes are required for each data-point.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
1. **Morton Index Calculation:** Compute the Morton index $M(r,g,b)$ for each voxel's color/value using bit-interleaving of its components [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the Morton index M(r,g,b) is computed for each voxel's color/value using bit-interleaving of its components. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'This ordering scheme allows us to compute the index of any given n-dimensional vector (here the RGB color) using simple bitshift operations.' In the context of Morton codes (Z-order curves), computing indices using bitshift operations is the standard implementation of bit-interleaving. Furthermore, the evidence confirms that M(r,g,b) represents the Morton index of the color (RGB). Therefore, every fact in the claim is supported by the evidence.
supported
3. **Noise Cleaning:** Identify colors present in the background images and set $h(r,g,b) = 0$ for all such colors to exclude background noise from storage [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that background noise is cleaned by identifying colors in background images and setting the histogram value h(r,g,b) to 0 for those colors. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'The histogram entries of all the colors found in the background-images are set to zero, excluding them from further processing during the encoding/storing step.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
It addresses the challenge of rendering large volumetric datasets that do not fit in main memory by organizing data on disk to minimize I/O latency [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the evidence addresses the challenge of rendering large volumetric datasets that do not fit in main memory by organizing data on disk to minimize I/O latency. The provided text explicitly describes an 'out-of-core approach' (which implies data does not fit in main memory) and details a data organization scheme using Morton order to store data on disk. The text further explains that this organization allows for accessing voxelsets in a consecutive manner to 'avoid unnecessary seek operations' and 'reduce seek/read operations,' which directly corresponds to minimizing I/O latency.
supported
- Degenerate input: If a color has zero occurrences after cleaning, it is excluded from the look-up table and file [S1, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states that to avoid storing unnecessary background noise, 'background-images' are used to clean the initial histogram. Specifically, 'The histogram entries of all the colors found in the background-images are set to zero, excluding them from further processing during the encoding/storing step.' This directly supports the claim that colors with zero occurrences (after this cleaning process) are excluded from the look-up table and file.
supported

It differs from standard Morton Code Encoding by integrating the spatial index with a histogram-based look-up table to manage variable-sized voxelsets on disk, enabling efficient out-of-core retrieval [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method differs from standard Morton Code Encoding by integrating a spatial index with a histogram-based look-up table to manage variable-sized voxelsets on disk for efficient out-of-core retrieval. Source [S1] explicitly describes: 1) Using Morton order (spatial index) to sort voxel indices based on spatial locality. 2) Generating a histogram h of occurrences. 3) Constructing a look-up table l based on this histogram to calculate starting offsets s_V for each voxelset. 4) Storing data at these offsets to manage variable-sized voxelsets on disk. 5) Using this structure for out-of-core retrieval by accessing files consecutively to reduce seek operations. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
- Background images used to identify noise colors [S1, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'To avoid storing unnecessary background noise data, we use “background-images” to clean up the initial histogram... The histogram entries of all the colors found in the background-images are set to zero'. This confirms that background images are used to identify which colors constitute noise (by setting their histogram entries to zero) for the purpose of excluding them from storage.
supported
- **Memory Complexity:** Requires storing the histogram and look-up table in memory [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that a histogram 'h' is generated and used as a base for a look-up table 'l' during the pre-processing phase. It further explains that the look-up table is generated using the histogram and is used for retrieving voxelsets. Since these data structures (histogram and look-up table) are created and utilized for the algorithm's operation (calculating offsets and retrieving data), the claim that the method requires storing them in memory is supported by the text describing the pre-processing and retrieval logic.
supported
- Voxel data including position (3×4-byte values) and normalized gradient (3 bytes) [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that voxel data includes position (3x4-byte values) and normalized gradient (3 bytes). Source [S1], in section 3.3 'Data Encoding', explicitly states: 'Assuming that we have three four-byte values for position and three bytes for normal-information, 15 bytes are required for each data-point.' This directly confirms the structure and byte sizes mentioned in the claim.
supported
- A 3D grid of voxels with dimensions $2^n \times 2^n \times 2^n$ [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in Source [S1] passages that the Morton order is constructed for an 'm-dimensional structure with {2^n}^m elements, where 2^n is the length of an edge'. For a 3D grid, the dimension m is 3, resulting in dimensions of 2^n x 2^n x 2^n. The claim accurately reflects this fact found in the text.
supported
- A look-up table $l$ mapping Morton indices to file offsets [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that a look-up table $l$ is generated using the histogram $h$ by successively adding the number of bytes needed to store a voxelset on disk to calculate starting offsets $s_V$. It further defines $s_V$ (the starting position/offset) using a formula involving the Morton index $M(r,g,b)$. Thus, the table maps Morton indices (via the color/voxelset identification) to file offsets.
supported

Morton Order Indexing for Out-of-Core Rendering is a data organization scheme that sorts voxel indices based on spatial locality using a recursive Z-shaped curve traversal, reducing disk seek operations by storing similar color/function values contiguously [S1, unofficial].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. The source explicitly describes Morton Order Indexing as a data organization scheme that sorts voxel indices based on spatial locality using a recursive Z-shaped curve traversal (specifically mentioning the 2D example of following a z-shaped curve within 2x2 squares recursively). It also states that this method reduces disk seek operations by storing similar color/function values contiguously, allowing for consecutive access and reduced seek/read operations.
supported
- **Strengths:** Exploits spatial locality for similar colors; reduces unnecessary disk rotations [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method exploits spatial locality for similar colors and reduces unnecessary disk rotations. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly confirms both points: 1) Under 'Data Retrieval', it states 'Similar selected colors are stored next to each other on disk' and 'By accessing the datasets in ascending order we exploit the following facts...'. 2) It also states that this access pattern allows performing 'just one disk-read operation... reducing the number of seek/read operations and avoiding unnecessary disk rotations.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
2. **Histogram Generation (Pass 1):** Iterate through all voxels and increment the histogram entry for each color/value: $h(r,g,b) \leftarrow h(r,g,b) + 1$ [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that in Pass 1, one iterates through all voxels and increments a histogram entry for each color/value. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'In the first pass, a histogram h is generated' and 'Generate a histogram h of contour value occurrences during the first pre-processing pass.' It further explains that this histogram contains 'the number of occurrences for each contour value' and is used to calculate offsets based on 'h(r,g,b)'. This confirms that the histogram is built by counting occurrences (incrementing entries) for each color/value during the first pass.
supported
- **Performance:** Reduces disk seek operations by accessing datasets consecutively, allowing real-time reading from disk [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method reduces disk seek operations by accessing datasets consecutively, allowing real-time reading. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the 'Data Retrieval' section: 'We avoid unnecessary seek operations by accessing datasets in a consecutive manner' and 'This type of data retrieval allows us to read the information from disk in real time.' The notes also corroborate that sorting by Morton order (spatial locality) reduces seek operations.
